items.title: How Metal Foam Could Make Cars Safer
items.summary: Once upon a time, cars were merely designed for performance, comfort, and usability, with little regard to how safe they may or may not be in the event of a collision. In this era, it turned out that most cars were horrific deathtraps, but eventually outside pressure led the industry to try and make cars safer. It was realized that making crashes more survivable with less injuries was generally a good thing. Ever since, there has been a general push towards making cars ever safer as time goes on. To that end, researchers have been exploring whether the use of metal foams could aid in further crash safety improvements. When it comes to automobile collisions, safety for vehicle occupants largely comes down to absorbing energy in a controlled manner. Vehicles moving at high speed have a great deal of kinetic energy, and that needs to be dissipated and controlled in such a way that the people inside a car are harmed as little as possible. The concept of crumple zones is key, here—wherein parts of the vehicle are designed to crumple and deform in such a way to absorb the energy of an impact while preserving the integrity of the passenger compartment of the vehicle as much as possible. Researchers at NC State University have been exploring whether or not metal foams could further improve the safety of vehicles in collisions. Composite metal foams (CMFs) are a material that consists of hollow metal spheres embedded in a greater metallic matrix. This creates a structure that is both lightweight, and highly capable of absorbing compressive and impact forces. The study used computational models to determine whether incorporating these metal foams into front rail vehicle crash structures could improve their ability to absorb energy in a crash. items.title: New Super Magnets Turbocharge the Large Hadron Collider
items.summary: Although the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has been making many amazing discoveries since its 2008 inauguration, it’s necessary to regularly upgrade its components to push the LHC’s performance to unlock new discoveries, as well as to perform general maintenance. The LHC has just completed its third run, which lasted from 2022 to July of 2026. In the ongoing third shutdown phase the most exciting upgrade is likely to be the high-luminosity (HL) upgrade, that introduces more powerful superconducting magnets . In the paper by [S. Izquierdo Bermudez] et al. we can find all the details about manufacturing these new niobium-tin (Nb 3 Sn) superconducting magnets. Although these boost the achievable field strength to nearly 12 Tesla from the 8.3 T of the previous niobium-titanium (NbTi) magnets, the latter were rather pliable whereas Nb 3 Sn is brittle in its superconducting phase and thus needs to be formed after winding. As can be seen in the above photos, this means that three manufacturing steps are required, ranging from winding and curing (left), to the heat treatment (center) under an inert atmosphere in which the material enters the brittle superconducting phase, followed by impregnation with epoxy resin. In the paper it’s detailed in how many ways this can go wrong, ranging from contamination to incorrect winding and handling glitches. With enough trial-error-and-corrections they managed to create a number of coils that passed all tests, with the now debugged tooling being helpful in scaling up production. If everything goes well, the LHC will enter its fourth run as the brand-new HL-LHC project by 2030, with the 5-7.5 times higher luminosity meaning that far more collisions should occur within any timespan, and thus much more data should be produced in less time. items.title: ESP32 WIFI Jam Detector Finds the Raspberry
items.summary: We’ve seen plenty of ESP32 WiFi projects that test wifi systems with attacks such as Deauth, and even jamming. Today’s project is a bit different. [TheDigital1] created an ESP32 project that uses SDR to detect interference in the WiFi bands . The detector builds on the popular ESPARGOS ESP-SDR project that we have previously featured , to scan for any interference. The hardware is based on an ESP32-C5, so it covers both the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands. [TheDigital1] used a Waveshare ESP32-C5-Touch-LCD-3.5, but since the project is open source, you should be able to port it to other devices. The system doesn’t just detect noise. It can categorize the interference into four types: wideband, narrowband, pulsed wideband, and frequency-swept. [TheDigital1] notes that while the system can detect interference, it can’t detect intent, so it’s up to the user to determine if they have a leaky microwave or hackers trying to shut down their WiFi. The system works great as a portable standalone device. In fact, the interface is pretty slick. Connecting it to a PC via USB opens up even more features. It can be used with Home Assistant as a WiFi Jammer detector. It can even detect if a room is occupied by sensing the noise floor increase from humans moving around. In a plural but interconnected grid such as Europe’s, that frequency can drift around a nominal center value. To keep track of this, [Jeroen Brinkman] has created a grid monitor that can show long-term trends as well as instantaneous frequencies. Hardware-wise, it’s somewhat old-school, with an Arduino Uno and a ubiquitous 2×16 character LCD, but the interest here lies not in the microcontroller. Sensing mains frequency is fraught with spicy high-voltage danger if done directly, so [Jeroen] is performing the task using an optocoupler that toggles an interrupt pin on the Arduino. The monitor stores long-term data by the week, using only four bytes per week. items.title: It’s A NAS, For Sony Mavica Disks
items.summary: At the dawn of the consumer digital camera age, manufacturers tested this new market with a wide array of interesting and unorthodox designs. This era only lasted a few years before they moved toward making models that resembled the 35mm cameras the consumers were used to. Sony’s Mavica offerings were particularly unusual, because they eschewed Flash storage for the then-ubiquitous 3.5″ floppy disk. Where there are files, there might be a need to share them, so [Bigcrimping] has created floppy3.5. It’s a NAS for digital Mavica disks . Inside, along with the floppy drive, is an interesting dual-processor architecture. An RP2354 runs a Greaseweazle port and reads the floppy drive, to the extent that it can operate as a standalone Greaseweazle device through its USB port. An ESP32-S3 is hooked into the RP2354 via SPI and performs the tasks of decoding the raw floppy data, copying the resulting files to an SD card, and sharing the images over a web interface. There’s also a pleasingly retro display intended to look like a Walkman display of the same era. This is an interesting project, both for Mavica owners for whom it’s very cool indeed, and as a portable Greaseweazle peripheral in its own right. More than once, we’ve had a random old floppy for which this appliance would have been a huge time saver. As we said earlier this year, it’s now imperative that you copy that floppy! items.summary: Do you need a 486-based handheld computer for DOS games? Well, we didn’t think so either — until we saw [Sprite_tm]’s impressive and excellently documented VapourDeck homebrew handheld PC. Now we want one for Christmas and to be [Sprite_tm] when we grow up. There exist industrial single-board computers designed around the Intel 486, and you’d be forgiven for thinking that’s what lives inside this build– but no. [Sprite_tm] was tired of thinking of a motherboard as “deep magic” and decided it was high time he designed his own. He chose the 486 because Intel actually let mere mortals at the documentation in those days, and it would let him play all his favourite DOS games on the fly. The board contains a period-appropriate VGA chip — complete with whopping 1MB of VRAM!– though most of the glue logic, I/Om and sound are on a modern FPGA and ESP32-S3, respectively. The writeup gives a good idea of the thinking behind this machine, but if you want to build one yourself, you can get all the files on Codeburg , because [Sprite_tm] was kind enough to open-source his work even if he’s not sure anyone else would want to replicate it. items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: Securing Your Agents: A Hands-On Guide to Agent Anomaly Detection
items.summary: This guide walks developers through setting up Agent Anomaly Detection on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform to monitor AI agent telemetry and catch behavioral risks. It demonstrates how to deploy a sample customer support agent, trigger out-of-scope security findings, and configure proactive alerts using Cloud Monitoring and Security Command Center.

items.title: How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection (AAD) provides asynchronous, low-latency monitoring for AI agents by analyzing OpenTelemetry traces and logs to flag goal hijacks and tool misuse. Tested across five public security benchmarks, AAD successfully caught 87% of harmful instructions carried out by agents without adding runtime latency. Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

items.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
items.summary: How pairing Go's surviving compiler bounds-check traps with Gemini 4 Argon and the Z3 constraint solver catches latent out-of-bounds panics in Go code and uncovers a slice-capacity blind spot in go test -fuzz.

items.title: A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences
items.summary: A2UI 1.0 is an open protocol for generative UI that enables AI agents to render interactive, native screens across web, mobile, and desktop applications. Developers can leverage open-source renderer SDKs—including React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose—alongside agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. The release introduces bidirectional function calls, swappable inference formats, and secure data binding to help teams seamlessly integrate generative UI into their product stacks.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: From prompt to app: Build with Google Maps in AI Studio
items.summary: Developers can now build applications powered by Google Maps Platform directly within Google AI Studio by prompting Gemini with real-world geospatial concepts. The integration eliminates traditional configuration hurdles by providing one-click demo keys that generate instantly without requiring Cloud Console redirects or credit cards. This setup grants developers immediate access to core APIs—including Maps, Places, and Routes—supported by daily sandbox quotas for seamless prototyping.

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

This integration preserves native file fidelity for use with Git repositories and developer tools while unlocking standard Docs features like line-level commenting, rendered Drive previews, and tracked version history.
